books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Democratic conventions of 1860 as told in Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 7, Topic 5.7, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 14. Dates and the walkout verified against the 1860 Democratic National Conventions record (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_Democratic_National_Conventions) and the OSU eHistory chronology. The facts are as stated in the books; the wording is original.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase: In April 1860 the Democrats met at Charleston, South Carolina, to choose a presidential candidate. Stephen A. Douglas led the voting, but Southern delegates demanded a platform promising that the federal government would protect slavery in the territories. When the convention refused, delegates from eight Southern states walked out, and the convention broke up without naming a nominee. The party met again in Baltimore in June and split in two: Northern Democrats nominated Douglas, and Southern Democrats nominated Vice President John C. Breckinridge.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Which of the following best explains why the split described in the passage helped Lincoln win the presidency?

options.text: Douglas and Breckinridge both campaigned for Lincoln.
options.misconception: Background: Douglas and Breckinridge ran against Lincoln; neither man campaigned for him.

options.text: Southern voters cast their ballots for Lincoln in large numbers.
options.misconception: Background: Lincoln won almost no votes in the Deep South and was not on the ballot in ten Southern states.

options.text: The split gave Lincoln a majority of the popular vote.
options.misconception: Background: Lincoln won under 40 percent of the popular vote; the split gave him electoral votes, not a popular majority.

options.text: Lincoln could win Northern states with pluralities instead of majorities.

rationales.A: Background: Douglas and Breckinridge ran against Lincoln; neither man campaigned for him.
rationales.B: Background: Lincoln won almost no votes in the Deep South and was not on the ballot in ten Southern states.
rationales.C: Background: Lincoln won under 40 percent of the popular vote; the split gave him electoral votes, not a popular majority.
rationales.D: With two Democrats dividing the opposition, Lincoln needed only more votes than any one rival in each Northern state. Background: he won the populous North state by state, and those electoral votes added up to 180.
rationales.general:
1. The passage leaves two Democrats facing one Republican.
2. In a winner-take-all state, a plurality takes all the electors.
3. Background: Lincoln's Northern pluralities piled up into 180 electoral votes.
4. The split did not make Lincoln popular; it made him first past the post.
Remember: in a four-way race, ask who must beat whom in each state, not who leads the nation.
